newsitem.title: USA: FBI says 25-agent team probes Democratic fundraiser.
newsitem.headline: FBI says 25-agent team probes Democratic fundraiser.

text.p: A 25-agent FBI task force has been assigned to investigate activities involving former Democratic fund-raiser John Huang, FBI Director Louis Freeh said in a letter made public on Tuesday.

Freeh said in the letter to Representative Gerald Solomon, a New York Republican, that more agents would be assigned if necessary to look into "complex issues involving significant economic and national security interests."

Solomon had asked Freeh for a probe into activities of Huang, a former top fund-raiser of the Democratic National Committee and previously a Commerce Department official. Huang is at the centre of a fund-raising controversy involving the Democratic Party that is under investigation by the Justice Department and will be the focus of congressional hearings.
"I have assigned 25 agents full-time and will provide whatever additional resources and support are needed as the investigation develops," Freeh wrote Solomon.

Last year, Attorney General Janet Reno rejected requests to appoint a special prosecutor to delve into the foreign contributions matters. Instead she said a Justice Department task force would look into allegations of possible wrongdoing.

In his letter to Freeh last week, Solomon said he wanted an investigation into possible compromising of U.S. economic and national security interests. He said he was not accusing Huang of anything illegal but expressed concern about possible misuse of a top secret security clearance by Huang to gain information on China during intelligence briefings while he was a Commerce Department official.

Solomon expressed concern about Huang receiving a top secret security clearance in January 1994, five months before he left the employment of the Lippo Group, an Indonesian financial conglomerate, to join the Commerce Department.

He said he was concerned that Huang "did not set aside his loyalties" to the Lippo organisation after he went to the Commerce Department as a deputy assistant secretary for international economic policy.
"There will be no lack of diligence on the FBI's part to investigate all of these matters thoroughly and as promptly as sound investigative practices permit," Freeh replied.

Huang, a naturalised American citizen of Chinese descent, left the Commerce Department on Jan. 17, 1996 and became a Democratic Party fundraiser who raised a reported $2.5 million for the party, much of it from Asian Americans and others with ties to foreign businesses.

The party has voluntarily returned funds that were deemed improperly raised from non-citizens and has also taken several steps to tighten its fund-raising practices, including an outright prohibition on accepting funds from foreigners.
The Los Angeles Times reported on Tuesday that the party received $27 million over two years from guests who attended coffee chats at the White House.

A computer analysis done for the newspaper showed many of those who attended the affairs with President Bill Clinton or administration officials "made substantial contributions to the Democratic Party within days of the events."
The White House has defended the affairs as appropriate, exposing Clinton to various views, and has denied they were designed to solicit funds.

"The pattern of donations suggests, however, that the 103 meetings between January 1995 and August 1996 were part of a system that cultivated major supporters who, in many cases, gave large contributions before or after attending the White House events," the Times said.

In another development, Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle said he did not want upcoming hearings on fund-raising matters to go into the 1998 congressional election year. He said he preferred to have the hearings over this year.
